title: Is the Dead Sea dead?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Dead Sea: its geography (lowest dry point on Earth, terminal lake fed by the Jordan River, shrinking by about a meter a year), its extreme salinity that makes swimmers float, claimed health benefits of its minerals and mud (studies on arthritis, fibromyalgia, psoriasis), the sea's lifelessness apart from halophilic bacteria, its biblical and historical ties (Dead Sea Scrolls found 1947-1956, Masada, Cleopatra), and the causes of its decline from diverted river water. They cover the proposed Two Seas Canal (Red Sea to Dead Sea, about five billion dollars, with desalination) and environmentalist alternatives like conservation and reduced agricultural use. The episode closes with a listener email from Shannon about life on Antarctic bases.

segments.title: Opening banter and the Dead Sea's irony
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter and introduce the Dead Sea as a geographical irony that is dying, noting it is about a meter lower each year and is a vanishing tourist attraction.

segments.title: Geography and salinity
segments.summary: The Dead Sea lies about 1,300 feet below sea level, is the lowest dry point on Earth, and is a terminal lake fed by the Jordan River with water leaving only by evaporation. Evaporation leaves mineral salts behind, making it one of the saltiest bodies of water, several times saltier than the saltiest ocean.

segments.title: Floating and health claims
segments.summary: The dense water lets people float easily. Companies sell Dead Sea minerals and mud products with health claims. Hosts cite published studies reporting benefits for arthritis, fibromyalgia, and skin conditions such as psoriasis, and describe the mud and spa tourism at the sea.

segments.title: Life, history, and the Dead Sea Scrolls
segments.summary: The sea supports almost no life except halophilic bacteria. Historical notes include the ancient name 'stinky Sea', asphalt, Cleopatra, King Herod and Masada. The hosts discuss the Dead Sea Scrolls found near the sea from 1947 to 1956, dated from the third century BC to the second century AD.

segments.title: Causes of decline and the Two Seas Canal
segments.summary: River diversion for agriculture and water use has reduced inflow from about 1.3 billion cubic meters a day in the 1950s to about 50 million now. A proposed Red Sea to Dead Sea canal, estimated at about five billion dollars with a desalination plant, is controversial. Environmentalists propose conservation and less agricultural use instead, and a study is underway.

segments.summary: Short sponsor read for a camera, followed by a plug for the Dead Sea search on the website.

segments.title: Listener mail on Antarctic bases
segments.summary: A listener named Shannon, who has spent summers at Antarctic bases, says life there is comfortable, with stores, bars, saunas, libraries, a food-focused culture, and medical facilities that can handle emergency surgery.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to get in touch by Twitter, Facebook, or email, and close the show.
